Rufford
RUF-urd
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Nottinghamshire, founded 1146 as a daughter of Rievaulx; its ranges became a great country house)
Old English ruh, rough, and ford: the rough ford. A Sherwood place name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Rufford was founded in 1146 on the edge of Sherwood, a daughter of Rievaulx, and was never large. At the dissolution it was granted to the Earl of Shrewsbury, whose family turned the west range into a country house; the Savile family enlarged it, and Rufford Abbey spent four centuries as a gentleman's seat before passing to the county council as a park. Its history is the commonest English fate of these houses, and it is the one that should make a Protestant least comfortable, because the dissolution was not chiefly a reformation of doctrine at Rufford — it was a transfer of land to men who wanted it. Scripture has a settled view of that kind of transaction, and it does not soften for a godly pretext. “Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!” (Isa 5:8); “And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage” (Mic 2:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines covet as to desire inordinately, to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess; dissolution as the act of dissolving, the breaking up of an assembly; and estate as property in land, or a fortune.

expand to see more

COVET, v.t. To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess; in a bad sense.

DISSOLUTION, n. The act of dissolving or separating the parts; the breaking up of an assembly, or the putting an end to it.

ESTATE, n. Property in land or real estate; also, fortune; possessions; property in general.

GRANT, n. The act of granting or conveying; also, the thing granted or bestowed; a gift; a boon.

OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity, rigor or hardship.

Key Scripture

Isa 5:8 — "Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!"

Mic 2:2 — "And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage."

Exo 20:17 — "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's."

1Ki 21:19 — "And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine."

Modern Corruption

A small Nottinghamshire house of 1146 granted at the dissolution and lived in as a country seat for four centuries: a transfer of land dressed as a reformation.

expand to see more

The corruption to name here is on the Protestant side of the ledger, and honesty requires naming it. Whatever was wrong in the monasteries — and this dictionary has said at length what was — the English dissolution enriched a class of courtiers, and the tenth commandment does not exempt them: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's” (Exo 20:17). Ahab had a legal mechanism too, and Elijah met him with “Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” (1Ki 21:19).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a true cause does not sanctify a greedy means. A reformation of the church's doctrine was necessary; the particular English method of effecting it put a great deal of land into particular hands, and “so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage” (Mic 2:2) is the prophet's word for that.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English ruh ford, the rough ford; Hebrew chamad (H2530), to covet; Hebrew gazal (H1497), to seize by violence; Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness.

expand to see more

Old English ruh ford — the rough ford; a plain Sherwood topographic name.

Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to desire, covet; “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house” (Exo 20:17).

Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, seize; “and take them by violence” (Mic 2:2).

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage; what Naboth would not sell.

Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the desire for more; Paul calls it idolatry.

Usage

"“that lay field to field, till there be no place” (Isa 5:8) — the woe on accumulation of estates."

"“Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” (1Ki 21:19) — the prophet to a king with a legal title."

"“nor any thing that is thy neighbour's” (Exo 20:17) — the commandment that exempts no cause."
